Explain DNS cache poisoning and how Kaminsky's attack works.

DNS cache poisoning injects malicious DNS records into a recursive resolver's cache, redirecting users to attacker-controlled IPs. Traditional attack: send forged DNS responses hoping to win race against legitimate response. Low success rate due to need to match transaction ID. Kaminsky attack (2008): exploits that resolvers cache NS records for entire zones. Attack: 1) Query resolver for non-existent subdomain (random.target.com). 2) Resolver queries target.com's NS. 3) Flood resolver with thousands of forged responses, each guessing 16-bit transaction ID (65535 possibilities). 4) Include forged NS record pointing target.com to attacker's server. 5) Once one response matches, resolver caches malicious NS for entire target.com zone. Critical: no need to re-attack for each query — cache the NS and own all queries to the zone. Mitigation: port randomization (adds ~16 bits of entropy), DNSSEC (cryptographic signing of DNS records), DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (prevents observation and modification in transit). Partial mitigation: 0x20 encoding (randomize case in query, legitimate server mirrors it). Complete mitigation: DNSSEC deployment, but adoption remains low.

How do you find and exploit SSRF vulnerabilities?

Server-Side Request Forgery causes a server to make HTTP requests to an attacker-specified location. The server's requests have internal network access the attacker lacks directly. Detection: any parameter that contains a URL or hostname — webhook URLs, file import URLs, PDF generators, URL preview features, image processing. Basic test: replace URL with http://attacker.com and observe if your server receives a request. Internal network access: http://192.168.1.1/admin, http://10.0.0.1:8080. Common internal services: http://localhost:6379 (Redis — often unauth), http://169.254.169.254 (AWS metadata service — contains IAM credentials), http://localhost:27017 (MongoDB). AWS IMDSv1 full exploit: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ returns role name, then /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE_NAME returns temporary AWS keys. Cloud-critical vulnerability. Bypass techniques: http://[::1]:80 (IPv6 localhost), http://127.0.0.1:80@evil.com (URL parser confusion), http://0.0.0.0:80, DNS rebinding (domain resolves to 127.0.0.1 after allowlist check), protocol switching (file://, gopher://, dict://, ftp://). Gopher protocol enables arbitrary TCP packet construction for Redis exploitation.
